entry: American singer and actor. One of the first multimedia stars, he made over 70 feature films and recorded more than 1,600 songs. He won the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Actor for *Going My Way* (1944) and was the number one box office attraction for five consecutive years, from 1944 to 1948. With his friend [[Bob Hope]], he starred in the *Road to* series of films from 1940 to 1962. Crosby influenced the development of the post–World War II recording industry. After seeing a German reel-to-reel tape recorder, he invested $50,000 in the California electronics company Ampex to build copies, and he became the first performer to prerecord his radio shows and master his commercial recordings onto [[Magnetic tape|magnetic tape]]. He co-owned the Pittsburgh Pirates, whose two [[World Series]] wins, in 1960 and 1971, came during that period.

Optical instrument made of two identical refracting telescopes mounted side by side and pointed in the same direction, giving magnified vision for both [[Eye|eyes]]. Unlike a monocular telescope, binoculars produce a three-dimensional image, because each eyepiece presents a slightly different view and [[Parallax|parallax]] lets the visual cortex generate an impression of depth. Most are held with both hands, though sizes range from small opera glasses to large pedestal-mounted tower viewers. Early binoculars used Galilean optics, with a convex objective and a concave eyepiece [[Lens|lens]]; this gave an erect image but a narrow field of view and limited magnification. Keplerian optics achieved higher magnification but inverted the image, which had to be corrected with erecting lenses or [[Prism (optics)|prisms]]. Ignazio Porro patented a prism erecting system in 1854, and in 1894 the Carl Zeiss company introduced improved "modern" Porro prism binoculars, whose well-separated, offset objectives gave a better sensation of depth.

Number of ways to choose an unordered subset of k elements from a set of n elements. Written C(n, k) or read as n choose k, it is the coefficient of the xᵏ term in the expansion of (1 + x)ⁿ, and it equals n!/(k!(n−k)!). Binomial coefficients are [[Integer|integers]] that appear in the successive rows of [[Pascal's triangle]]. For example, there are six ways to choose two elements from {1, 2, 3, 4}.

Discrete [[Probability distribution|probability distribution]] of the number of successes in a sequence of n independent yes–no experiments, each with success probability p. The probability of exactly k successes is [[Binomial coefficient|C(n, k)]]pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ, and the [[Expected value|expected value]] is np. A single trial is a [[Bernoulli distribution|Bernoulli distribution]]. The distribution is frequently used to model successes in a sample drawn with replacement from a population, and it remains a good approximation for sampling without replacement when the population is much larger than the sample. It is the basis of the binomial test of [[Statistics|statistical]] significance. [[Jacob Bernoulli]] formalized it in his posthumous 1713 work *Ars Conjectandi*, and Abraham de Moivre developed its [[Normal distribution|normal approximation]] in 1733.

Formal system of naming [[Species|species]] with a two-part name in [[Latin]] form, such as *Homo sapiens* for modern humans. The first part, the generic name, identifies the [[Genus|genus]]; the second, the specific epithet, distinguishes the species within it. [[Carl Linnaeus]] formally introduced the system in *Species Plantarum* (1753), though Gaspard Bauhin had used many genus names later adopted by Linnaeus as early as 1622. Binomial names were designed to be succinct, relatively stable, verifiable and understood internationally, unlike common names, which differ in every language. The International Code of Zoological Nomenclature governs animals, and the International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants governs plants and fungi. In modern usage the genus name is capitalized and both parts are italicized.

Formula for the algebraic expansion of powers of a binomial. For a nonnegative integer n, (x + y)ⁿ is the sum of terms C(n, k)xⁿ⁻ᵏyᵏ for k from 0 to n, where each coefficient is a [[Binomial coefficient|binomial coefficient]]. For example, (x + y)⁴ = x⁴ + 4x³y + 6x²y² + 4xy³ + y⁴. The coefficients form the nth row of [[Pascal's triangle]]. In the 1660s [[Isaac Newton]] generalized the theorem to fractional and negative exponents, producing an infinite [[Series (mathematics)|series]].

Arboreal viverrid mammal of South and Southeast Asia, also known as the bearcat. It is the only species in the genus *Arctictis*, and nine subspecies have been proposed. It has long, thick, mostly dark hair, a bushy prehensile tail, and musk glands that smell of [[Popcorn|popcorn]]. An omnivore that feeds on plants, insects and smaller animals, it is primarily nocturnal, and females can delay implantation until conditions are favorable. Habitat loss, forest degradation and illegal hunting and trading threaten it, and it is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List.

2007 first-person shooter [[Video game|video game]]. Developed by 2K Boston (later Irrational Games) and published by 2K, *BioShock* was released for Microsoft Windows and [[Xbox 360]] in August 2007, with a PlayStation 3 port in October 2008. The player explores Rapture, an underwater [[Utopia|utopia]] built by businessman Andrew Ryan, whose decline began after the discovery of ADAM, a substance that grants superhuman powers. Critics praised its narrative, themes, setting and gameplay. Two sequels followed, *BioShock 2* (2010) and *BioShock Infinite* (2013).

Fuel produced from biomass over a short time span, rather than by the very slow natural processes that form [[Fossil fuel|fossil fuels]]. Mostly used for transportation, biofuels are regarded as a [[Renewable energy|renewable energy]] source. The two most common types are [[Ethanol|bioethanol]], an alcohol made by fermentation mostly from sugar and starch crops such as [[Maize|maize]] and [[Sugarcane|sugarcane]], and biodiesel, such as that made from canola or soybeans. The United States is the largest bioethanol producer and the EU the largest biodiesel producer. Climate impact varies with feedstock, production and land-use change, and in some scenarios biofuel emissions are comparable to fossil fuels. Critics cite the "food vs fuel" debate and the [[Deforestation|deforestation]] linked to production. Global consumption is projected to grow by an average of 1.4% annually between 2026 and 2035.

Detailed written account of a person's life, presenting the subject's experience beyond basic facts such as education, work and death. Biographies are usually [[Non-fiction|non-fiction]], though fiction can portray a life. An authorized biography is written with the subject's or heirs' permission, while an [[Autobiography|autobiography]] is written by its subject, sometimes with a ghostwriter. The genre began as a subsection of history and emerged as a distinct genre in the 18th century. Biography is considered the earliest literary genre, and its first texts are funerary inscriptions from the 26th century BC recounting the careers of officials. [[Plutarch]]'s *Parallel Lives*, published about 80 AD, paired famous Greeks with Romans, such as [[Demosthenes]] and [[Cicero]]. In the early Middle Ages, biographies mostly concerned church fathers, martyrs, [[Pope|popes]] and [[Saint|saints]], often written to inspire and to convert people to [[Christianity]].

Natural science discipline of anthropology concerned with the biological and behavioral aspects of human beings, their extinct hominin ancestors, and related non-human [[Primate|primates]], from an evolutionary perspective. Also called physical anthropology, it is divided into branches including bioarchaeology, evolutionary psychology, forensic anthropology, human biology, paleoanthropology and primatology. Forensic anthropology applies human osteology to legal cases, most often criminal cases in which the victim's remains are in advanced decomposition. Biological anthropologists regard the work of [[Charles Darwin]] as a major foundation for the field.

Substance produced by living organisms whose color results from selective absorption of light. Pigment color is the same from every viewing angle, unlike structural color, which results from selective reflection or iridescence. Pigments occur in skin, eyes, [[Feather|feathers]], fur and hair, often as [[Melanin|melanin]] in specialized cells called chromatophores. In plants the primary pigment is [[Chlorophyll|chlorophyll]], which absorbs blue and red light while reflecting most green; all land plants and green algae contain chlorophyll a and b. [[Carotenoid|Carotenoids]] are red, orange or yellow, and act as accessory pigments in [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]]. [[Anthocyanin|Anthocyanins]] are water-soluble pigments that appear red to blue according to [[PH|pH]]. Changes in pigment can also signal to pollinators which flowers are rewarding.

Use of living organisms or their toxins, such as bacteria, viruses, insects or fungi, to kill, harm or incapacitate humans, animals or plants as an act of war. Offensive use in international armed conflicts is a war crime under the 1925 Geneva Protocol, and the 1972 Biological Weapons Convention bans the development, production, stockpiling and use of such weapons while permitting defensive research. Biological warfare is distinct from [[Chemical weapon|chemical]], nuclear and radiological warfare, and some agents, such as [[Smallpox|smallpox]] and pneumonic [[Plague (disease)|plague]], can spread from person to person. Japan's Imperial Army, through [[Unit 731]], tested plague, [[Anthrax|anthrax]] and cholera on Chinese civilians and prisoners during [[World War II]], resulting in tens of thousands of deaths. After World War II, the [[Soviet Union]] and the United States developed offensive programs amid [[Cold War]] tensions.

Distinct geographical region with a specific climate, vegetation and animal life, consisting of a biological community that has formed in response to its physical environment and regional climate. The International Biological Program (1964–74) projects popularized the concept. In 1935 Arthur Tansley added climatic and soil aspects to the idea, calling it [[Ecosystem|ecosystem]]. Because the change from one biome to another is gradual, boundaries must be drawn arbitrarily. Classification schemes differ: Leslie Holdridge (1947) used temperature and rainfall to define 30 "humidity provinces", and Robert Whittaker used precipitation and temperature in a simpler scheme. Principal biome types include [[Tundra|tundra]], [[Taiga|taiga]], deciduous [[Forest|forest]], [[Grassland|grasslands]], [[Desert|desert]] and tropical forest.

Branch of biophysics that applies the methods of mechanics to the structure, function and motion of biological systems. It operates at every level, from whole organisms to organs, [[Cell (biology)|cells]], [[Organelle|cell organelles]] and even proteins. Biofluid mechanics studies gas and liquid flows in or around organisms, such as [[Blood|blood]] flow, which can be modeled by the [[Navier–Stokes equations]]. Biotribology studies [[Friction|friction]], wear and lubrication in biological systems, especially human joints such as hips and knees. Comparative biomechanics applies the field to non-human organisms, most often for [[Animal locomotion|animal locomotion]], while computational biomechanics uses tools such as the finite element method. In medicine, the field informs orthopedic implant design and gait analysis for rehabilitation.

Application of [[Engineering|engineering]] principles and design concepts to medicine and biology for healthcare purposes, such as diagnosis and [[Therapy|therapy]]. Biomedical engineers develop biocompatible prostheses, diagnostic and therapeutic devices, micro-implants, imaging technologies such as MRI and EKG/ECG, regenerative tissue growth, and pharmaceutical drugs including biopharmaceuticals. The field also covers managing hospital medical equipment through procurement, routine testing and preventive maintenance; this role is also called a biomedical equipment technician or clinical engineer. Subfields include [[Biomechanics|biomechanics]], biomaterials science and biomedical optics, which underpins techniques such as optical coherence tomography. Key historical achievements include the [[X-ray]] machine, the electrocardiograph and the pacemaker.

Molecule produced by a living organism and essential to one or more biological processes. Biomolecules include large [[Carbohydrate|carbohydrates]], [[Protein|proteins]], [[Lipid|lipids]] and [[Nucleic acid|nucleic acids]], as well as small molecules such as [[Vitamin|vitamins]] and [[Hormone|hormones]]. Most are organic compounds; oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen alone make up 96% of the human body's mass. [[DNA]] usually forms a double helix in which C pairs with G and A with T, while RNA forms large, complex three-dimensional structures. Nucleotides supply chemical energy in the form of [[Adenosine triphosphate|adenosine triphosphate]] and participate in cellular signaling. The uniformity of certain biomolecules and metabolic pathways across all life is known as the theory of material unity of living beings, or "biochemical universals".

Medical test that extracts cells or tissue from the body for examination to determine the presence or extent of disease. The sample is typically fixed, sectioned, stained and examined under a [[Microscope|microscope]] by a pathologist, and may also be analyzed chemically. Incisional and core biopsies sample part of an abnormal area, excisional biopsies remove an entire lump, and fine needle aspiration collects cells without preserving tissue architecture. Biopsies are most often performed to investigate possible [[Cancer|cancer]] or inflammation, and pathologists use them to distinguish benign from malignant lesions. Liquid biopsies, which test [[Blood|blood]] or urine for cancer cells or substances they release, offer a noninvasive way to monitor treatment. The term combines the Greek words for "life" and "sight", and the French dermatologist Ernest Besnier introduced it in 1879.

Worldwide sum of all [[Ecosystem|ecosystems]] on Earth, also called the ecosphere and described as the zone of life on Earth. It is virtually a closed system for matter but an open system for energy, as [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]] captures solar energy at a rate of around 100 terawatts. The biosphere integrates all living beings with the [[Lithosphere|lithosphere]], [[Cryosphere|cryosphere]], hydrosphere and atmosphere, and is thought to have evolved at least 3.5 billion years ago. Geologist Eduard Suess coined the term in 1875 for the place on Earth's surface where life dwells. Vladimir Vernadsky developed the concept in the 1920s and defined [[Ecology|ecology]] as the science of the biosphere. The total number of living cells on Earth is estimated at 10³⁰. Artificial biospheres such as Biosphere 2 are studied as closed, self-regulating systems.

Form of terrestrial locomotion in which an animal moves on its two rear limbs. Several groups of modern species are habitual bipeds, including [[Bird|birds]], which are members of a clade of exclusively bipedal [[Dinosaur|dinosaurs]], and among mammals the macropods, kangaroo rats, pangolins and hominins, including [[Human|humans]]. Bipedalism raises the head for a wider field of vision and frees the forelimbs for manipulation, flight, digging or combat. According to the [[Running|endurance running]] hypothesis, bipedalism allowed humans to outrun most other animals over long distances. Hominin fossils such as [[Lucy (hominid)|Lucy]] (*Australopithecus afarensis*), about 3.2 million years old, show upright [[Walking|walking]].

Mood disorder on the [[Bipolar disorder|bipolar spectrum]], involving at least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode, but never a full [[Mania|manic]] episode. Hypomanic episodes last at least four days. Depressive episodes are usually more frequent and intense, and the disorder carries a greater risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors than bipolar I disorder or unipolar depression. It is often underdiagnosed, because patients usually seek help when depressed. Treatment typically combines [[Medication|medication]] with [[Psychotherapy|psychotherapy]].

[[Mental disorder|Mental disorder]] marked by periods of depression and abnormally elevated mood, previously known as manic depression. Elevated mood is called [[Mania|mania]] if it is severe or associated with [[Psychosis|psychosis]], and hypomania if it does not significantly affect functioning. Bipolar I disorder involves at least one manic episode, while [[Bipolar II disorder|bipolar II disorder]] involves at least one hypomanic episode and one major depressive episode. Genetic factors may account for up to 70–90% of the risk, and identical twins both have the disorder at a rate of about 40%, compared with about 5% for dizygotic twins. Mood stabilizers, anticonvulsants and atypical antipsychotics are used for treatment, and [[Psychotherapy|psychotherapy]] improves the course of the disorder. Antidepressants are controversial because some classes increase the risk of mania. People with the disorder are 11.7 times more likely to die by [[Suicide|suicide]] than the general population, although that estimate comes from studies with high heterogeneity.

Thin-leaved deciduous hardwood tree of the genus *Betula*, in the family Betulaceae, which also includes [[Alder|alders]], hazels and hornbeams. The genus contains 30 to 60 known taxa, 11 of which are on the 2011 IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Birches are typically short-lived pioneer species, widespread in the [[Northern Hemisphere|Northern Hemisphere]], particularly in northern temperate and boreal climates. Their [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is marked with long horizontal lenticels and often separates into papery plates, as in the paper birch. The close-grained wood takes a fine polish and is used for furniture, plywood and pulp. Indigenous peoples used paper birch bark for [[Canoe|canoes]] and containers.

Family of 44 species in 17 genera of [[Passerine|passerine]] birds found mainly in [[New Guinea|New Guinea]], [[Australia|eastern Australia]] and the [[Maluku Islands|Maluku Islands]]. Most live in dense [[Rainforest|rainforest]] habitats, and their diet is dominated by fruit, with some arthropods. Males of most species are [[Sexual dimorphism|sexually dimorphic]], with very long, elaborate feathers extending from the beak, wings, tail or head. Breeding systems range from monogamy to lek-type polygamy. The long tail feather of the greater bird-of-paradise is used as a decorative element in the Shripech, the royal crown of Nepalese monarchs. The closest relatives include the [[Corvidae|crow and jay family]]. Several species are threatened by hunting and habitat loss.

Hypercarnivorous bird that actively hunts and feeds on other [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]], also called a raptor. Birds of prey have keen eyesight, strong feet with sharp talons, and powerful curved beaks for tearing flesh, and many, such as [[Vulture|vultures]] and condors, also scavenge carrion. The term raptor derives from the Latin *rapio*, "to seize or take by force". [[Eagle|Eagles]] are large, powerful birds with long, broad wings and massive feet, while [[Falcon|falcons]] and kestrels are medium-sized and swift. True [[Accipiter|hawks]] mostly belong to the genus Accipiter. [[Owl|Owls]] are typically night-hunting birds that fly almost silently. The [[Osprey|osprey]] is a single species, found worldwide, that specializes in catching fish. Vultures form two families: the Old World vultures (Accipitridae) and the New World vultures (Cathartidae).
